stances.claim: Both ATA pros (Lacson, Duterte) and contras (Calleja, Luistro, Sta. Maria, Monsod, Arroyo) have placed admirable unanimous trust in the Supreme Court's impartiality and fairness -- making the magistrates themselves, not just the litigants and their positions, the central institutional question.
stances.rhetorical_move: trust-as-evidence framing (treating bipartisan reliance on the Court as proof of institutional legitimacy)

stances.claim: The petitioners' prayer to have judges (not executive officials) personally determine probable cause for ATA arrests is itself enduring proof of their faith in the judiciary -- they want the Court's protection because they trust it.
stances.rhetorical_move: petition-as-proof-of-trust (using the relief sought as evidence of underlying institutional faith)

stances.claim: It behooves the Court to be worthy of that trust by resolving the petitions on their merits rather than dismissing them on procedural defects (lack of cause of action, prematurity under Section 58), and to avoid producing perplexing dictums like Javellana (raising of hands), Atong Paglaum (party-list opened to the rich), Arroyo v People (main-plunderer requirement), or Republic v. Sereno (quo warranto ouster of a chief justice).
stances.rhetorical_move: merit-on-merit imperative + perplexing-dictums cautionary list (negative precedent as warning)

stances.claim: The Court must be impervious to 'the plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship' -- the social-network pressures that compromise institutional independence -- and stand by its convictions even when 'the mob rages against them, threatens their families, and chants slogans of hate.'
stances.rhetorical_move: named-pathology framing ('plague of ships' as memorable mnemonic for judicial-capture pressures)

stances.claim: Quoting Frankfurter via his 1999 book 'Leadership by Example,' the Court's only tools are courage, integrity, and sagacity -- it 'does not lust for the brute power of the executive' nor 'desire the patronage of the legislature,' and serves as the 'conscience of society' precisely by upholding basic norms against tyrants, lynch mobs, and 'best-intentioned but ill-informed crusaders.'
stances.rhetorical_move: Frankfurter-via-self-citation (anchoring institutional ideal in foreign authority quoted in CJ's own published work)

notable_anecdotes: Ninoy Aquino's refusal to participate 'in any manner' in Marcos's military tribunal -- invoked as the counter-example of when NOT to trust a tribunal, making the petitioners' decision to sue the Court itself implicit proof of judicial faith.

The 'plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship' -- one of CJ's most memorable named-pathology mnemonics, used here to warn against judicial capture by social-network pressures.

The four-case cautionary list of 'perplexing dictums' -- Javellana (1973 raising-of-hands ratification), Atong Paglaum (2013 party-list opened to the rich), Arroyo v People (2016 main-plunderer requirement), Republic v Sereno (2018 quo warranto ouster) -- the most concentrated single-paragraph indictment of past SC controversies in any of CJ's ATA columns.

CJ's extended self-quotation from 'Leadership by Example' (Supreme Court Printing Press, 1999), invoking Frankfurter's 'conscience of society' -- making the column an institutional-ideal manifesto rather than mere ATA commentary.

The crystalline final formula: 'It prays only for courage, integrity and sagacity, for these are its only tools with which to fulfill its work and to deserve the people's trust' -- one of CJ's most distilled statements of judicial virtue.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his Anti-Terror Act series by noting that 'never in a long while has a law generated more controversy' -- yet what is comforting is the admirable unanimity of both pros (Sen. Panfilo Lacson, President Duterte) and contras (Howard Calleja, Br. Armin Luistro, FEU Dean Mel Sta. Maria, ConCom's Christian Monsod and Felicitas Arroyo, minority solons) in their trust of the Supreme Court's impartiality and fairness. The contras' prayer to have judges, not executive officials, personally determine probable cause for ATA arrests is itself 'the enduring proof of their faith in the judiciary' -- they want the Court's protection because they trust it. The counter-example is the martyred Ninoy Aquino's refusal to participate in Marcos's military tribunal: had the petitioners doubted the Court, they would not have prayed for its intervention at all. Panganiban argues that the Court must be worthy of this bipartisan trust by ruling on the merits rather than dismissing on procedural niceties or prematurity under Section 58 -- and avoiding 'perplexing dictums' that have damaged its reputation: the raising of hands in barangay assemblies to ratify a Constitution (Javellana, 1973), opening the party-list to every Juan including the rich and powerful (Atong Paglaum, 2013), the main-plunderer identification requirement (Arroyo v. People, 2016), and the ousting of a chief justice via quo warranto (Republic v. Sereno, 2018). The justices must be impervious to 'the plague of ships: kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship.' He closes with an extended self-quotation from his 1999 book 'Leadership by Example,' invoking Justice Frankfurter's framing of the Court as 'the conscience of society,' and concluding that 'the Court does not lust for the brute power of the executive. Neither does it desire to have the patronage of the legislature. It prays only for courage, integrity and sagacity, for these are its only tools with which to fulfill its work and to deserve the people's trust.'
